title: A Private Army by Barge: Homestead, Three Congressional Inquiries, and a Statute That Bound Only the Government
participants: Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers
Senate Committee on Education and Labor

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Carnegie Steel’s chairman Henry Clay Frick moves to break the Amalgamated Association’s contract at Homestead in 1892; the wage scale the lockout replaces is the standing cost the company means to remove.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: Rather than municipal or state police, the company contracts a private firm. About three hundred armed Pinkerton men are brought up the Monongahela by barge on 6 July 1892, and the landing becomes a gun battle that kills men on both sides.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fight is argued as a riot by workmen rather than as a corporation deploying a private armed force, and the Pennsylvania militia occupies the town, which settles the plant’s operation long before any inquiry reports.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The union is driven out of Homestead and out of the steel industry for a generation; the labour cost the lockout targeted stays removed.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Three congressional investigations take evidence — the House Judiciary Committee’s hearings, its report of 7 February 1893, and a Senate select committee resolution — and the statutory answer, the Anti-Pinkerton proviso of 3 March 1893, forbids the federal government from employing such an agency. It says nothing about a corporation hiring one against its own workforce. Prosecutions on both sides, including treason charges against strike leaders, end in no convictions.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The nineteenth-century practice of corporations retaining private detective agencies as guards, strikebreakers and informants, with no statute addressing the arrangement.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The congressional-inquiry-plus-narrow-statute pattern: a public investigation of a private armed force, answered by a rule that binds only federal hiring and leaves the private market for armed contractors intact.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The agency keeps the contract market; the company keeps the wage reduction; the record of the inquiry becomes the public settlement of the matter, and the next corporation hires guards under the same law.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: Homestead as a spontaneous riot — a mob of armed strikers attacking watchmen hired to protect a mill — or, in the other telling, as a one-off outrage already answered by the Anti-Pinkerton Act.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Congress investigated the arrangement itself, three times in seven months: a House Judiciary hearing volume, a House report, and a Senate resolution for a select committee on the employment of "Pinkerton men". The statute that followed reaches federal hiring only, so the practice it is said to have ended continued in private hands.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A corporation contracted roughly three hundred armed men and landed them by barge at its own plant; the state then supplied the militia; three congressional records (H. Misc. Doc. 52-335, H. Rept. 52-2447, S. Rept. 52-1105) document the employment of the agency; and the resulting proviso of 3 March 1893 restricted only the government’s own use of it.
